steps.prompt:
Time now: 2026-08-10 18:32 UTC

What the bot watches (context only, not a list to have ideas about):
  AAPL, JNJ, KO, MSFT, QQQ, SPY

Instrument classes. The watch list above is a starting point; this is a fence:
  crypto — BLOCKED. Do not name a symbol here and do not build a chain that only pays off through one.
  us_equity — ENABLED. Any symbol in this class is fair game, including ones not on the watch list.

A `symbols` entry must be something the broker can route inside an ENABLED class above: a listed US ticker or ETF, or a crypto pair such as BTC/USD. Anything else — a private company, a co-operative, an unlisted foreign producer, a commodity with no fund — is dropped before storage. Reason about those freely and name them in `instruments`; bridge to a listed instrument in a hop if one exists, and leave `symbols` empty if none does.

Produce one step. Advance one of the dreams above if any is worth advancing, otherwise start a new one.

Two fields decide whether this dream ever reaches anybody, so answer them deliberately:
  - `symbols`: the LISTED instrument this chain reaches, inside an enabled class. If what you are reasoning about is not listed, bridge to one that is and write that bridge as a hop. If there is no honest bridge, leave it empty — that is a respectable answer and much better than a proxy you would not trade.
  - `conditions`: what would have to be true before this is worth offering. A keep verdict with no checkable condition never leaves the workbench. Give each a sentence, and a symbol/field/op/value wherever the claim can carry one. The value is a number you read off the figures, never the name of another figure.
  - the WEAKEST HOP has to be covered. Name it, give its number in `weakest_hop_index`, and put that number in `settles_hops` on a checkable condition. A prophecy is a dream parked awaiting the link that could kill it; a threshold on a link nobody doubted settles nothing and the dream stays on the workbench. If no number could settle that hop, leave the dream on the workbench and say why.

model_returned.title: French heat, nuclear cooling limits, and who inherits the aluminium gap
model_returned.seed: August heat has, in past years, forced French nuclear plants to throttle output when river water gets too warm to use for cooling — and Europe's aluminium smelters are among the most power-hungry industries on that grid.
model_returned.thought: This is the same mechanism that hit in 2022, just asking whether it repeats. Every hop is checkable against a public record I have not actually pulled this week, so I am laying the chain out rather than claiming it fired.

chain.claim: French river temperatures rise in August, and regulations require EDF to curtail nuclear output when cooling-water discharge would exceed thermal limits.
When nuclear output is curtailed during peak summer demand, European wholesale electricity prices rise, as happened in prior heatwave summers.
European aluminium smelters are energy-intensive enough that several curtailed or idled production when power costs spiked in 2021-2022.
Reduced European smelter output tightens global aluminium supply and supports price for producers outside Europe.
Alcoa (AA), a listed US producer with no exposure to French grid pricing, benefits from a higher global aluminium price when a rival region's supply is impaired.

model_returned.weakest_hop: Whether this particular August is actually producing the river-temperature curtailments — that is the fact the whole chain depends on and I have not seen this month's EDF or RTE output data.
model_returned.trigger: An EDF or RTE announcement of nuclear output reduction tied to cooling-water limits before end of August, or its absence.

conditions.text: EDF or RTE publicly confirms a nuclear output curtailment this August attributed to river cooling-water limits.
A named European smelter (e.g. one of the Alcoa, Trimet or Rio Tinto European operations) announces a curtailment or output cut citing power costs.

chain.claim: Yunnan's aluminium smelters are heavily hydropower-dependent, and in 2021 and 2022 low reservoir levels led to provincial curtailment orders on aluminium production.
chain.source: public reporting on the 2021-2022 Yunnan hydropower and aluminium-curtailment episodes

chain.claim: Whether a comparable hydropower shortfall or curtailment order is occurring in Yunnan during the 2026 dry season is unverified — I have no current reservoir or output data.

If Chinese aluminium output is curtailed, global supply tightens and non-Chinese primary producers such as Alcoa (AA) could see the benefit in realised prices; how much of that is already priced into AA is unclear.

model_returned.title: Eggs at the margin
model_returned.seed: Bird flu culls flocks unevenly, and the ones left standing get to sell into the price the culling created.
model_returned.origin: Noticing that avian flu outbreaks recur seasonally and always seem to leave one producer looking lucky rather than unlucky.
model_returned.thought: Working through this one hop at a time before I decide if there's anything real here or if it's just a story I like the shape of.

chain.claim: USDA APHIS publishes HPAI (bird flu) detections and cull sizes by flock, state and date as public record.
US table-egg production is concentrated in a small number of very large layer operations, so a single cull removes a large slice of national supply at once.
Egg prices clear close to a national wholesale reference (Urner Barry-style index), so a producer whose flock is untouched sells into the post-cull price rather than at its own pre-cull cost.
Cal-Maine Foods describes itself as the largest US shell-egg producer in its own SEC filings, making it the natural beneficiary when a rival's flock is culled and its own is not.

model_returned.weakest_hop: The margin-windfall mechanism (hop 3) is the load-bearing claim, and I have no figure for how much of the price spike actually passes through to an unaffected producer versus being absorbed by feed cost, contracts, or hedging.

model_returned.title: Eggs at the margin
model_returned.seed: Bird flu culls flocks unevenly, and the ones left standing get to sell into the price the culling created.
model_returned.thought: Sitting with hop 3. The whole chain rests on an unaffected producer pocketing the post-cull price rather than its own pre-cull cost. Who already knows this? Everyone who reads a bird-flu headline knows egg prices spike — that part is priced into CALM within days of a cull announcement, probably before I could act on it. What I don't know, and haven't been shown, is how much of that spike survives as margin versus getting eaten by CALM's own feed costs, contracts and hedges. That's not a guess I should dress up with a made-up percentage. It needs CALM's own disclosed average selling price per dozen against its cost of production, which only shows up in their quarterly filings, not in a daily price series. Until I have that figure, hop 3 stays unverified and I shouldn't pretend a share-price threshold tests it — a stock move confirms the market believes the mechanism, not that the mechanism is real.
